chapters.title: Section 1: OF THE DIFFERENT SPECIES OF PHILOSOPHY.
paragraphs: 1. Moral philosophy, or the science of human nature, can be approached in two different ways, each with its own merit, and each capable of contributing to the entertainment, instruction, and reform of mankind. The first considers man chiefly as a being born for action, guided in his choices by taste and feeling, pursuing one object and avoiding another according to the value those objects seem to have and the light in which they appear. Since virtue, of all objects, is granted to be the most valuable, philosophers of this kind paint her in the most attractive colors, drawing every resource from poetry and eloquence and treating their subject in an easy, accessible way best suited to please the imagination and engage the affections. They pick out the most striking observations and examples from ordinary life, set opposing characters in pointed contrast, and, luring us into the paths of virtue with prospects of glory and happiness, guide our steps along those paths with the soundest precepts and most illustrious examples. They make us _feel_ the difference between vice and virtue; they stir and regulate our sentiments; and if they can bend our hearts toward integrity and true honor, they consider the goal of all their labor fully achieved.

2. The second kind of philosopher considers man as a reasoning rather than an acting being, and tries to develop his understanding more than to refine his manners. They treat human nature as a subject for theoretical inquiry and examine it with close scrutiny, looking for the principles that govern our understanding, stir our sentiments, and make us approve or condemn any particular object, action, or behavior. They see it as a reproach to all learning that philosophy has not yet settled, beyond dispute, the foundations of morals, reasoning, and criticism, and should still be debating truth and falsehood, vice and virtue, beauty and ugliness, without being able to identify the source of these distinctions. While they undertake this demanding task, no difficulties deter them. Moving from particular cases to general principles, they keep pressing their inquiries toward principles still more general, and are not satisfied until they reach those first principles by which, in every science, all human curiosity must be bounded. Although their reasonings seem abstract and even unintelligible to ordinary readers, they aim at the approval of the learned and the wise, and think themselves sufficiently rewarded for the labor of a lifetime if they can uncover some hidden truths that may contribute to the instruction of future generations.

3. It is certain that the easy and obvious philosophy will always, with most of mankind, be preferred over the precise and abstruse, and that many will recommend it not only as more agreeable but as more useful than the other. It enters more deeply into common life, shapes the heart and the affections, and, by touching the principles that move men, reforms their conduct and brings them closer to the model of perfection it describes. The abstruse philosophy, on the other hand, rests on a turn of mind that cannot engage with practical affairs, and so it vanishes when the philosopher leaves the shadows and steps into open day; nor can its principles easily keep any hold on our conduct and behavior. The feelings of the heart, the stirring of the passions, the force of the affections dissolve all its conclusions and reduce the profound philosopher to an ordinary man.

4. It must also be admitted that the most lasting, and the most deserved, fame has been won by the easy philosophy, and that abstract reasoners seem so far to have enjoyed only a brief reputation, owing to the caprice or ignorance of their own time, and have been unable to sustain their renown with a fairer posterity. It is easy for a deep thinker to make a mistake in his subtle reasonings; and one mistake is the inevitable parent of another, as he pushes his conclusions further and is not deterred from accepting any result, however strange or contrary to common opinion. But a philosopher who aims only to present the common sense of mankind in more beautiful and engaging colors, if he happens to fall into error, goes no further. By renewing his appeal to common sense and the natural sentiments of the mind, he returns to the right path and protects himself from any dangerous illusions. The fame of Cicero flourishes today; that of Aristotle has utterly faded. La Bruyère crosses borders and still holds his reputation, while the glory of Malebranche is confined to his own nation and his own age. And Addison, perhaps, will still be read with pleasure long after Locke has been entirely forgotten.

The mere philosopher is generally not very welcome in the world, since he is thought to contribute nothing to either the advantage or the pleasure of society, living apart from human contact and wrapped up in principles and ideas equally remote from ordinary comprehension. On the other hand, the merely ignorant man is despised even more; and in an age and nation where the sciences flourish, nothing is taken as a surer sign of a coarse mind than to have no taste at all for those noble pursuits. The most complete character is thought to lie between these extremes: combining an equal capacity and appetite for books, company, and business; bringing to conversation the discernment and refinement that come from cultivated reading; and bringing to business the integrity and accuracy that follow from sound philosophy. To spread and cultivate such a well-rounded character, nothing is more useful than writings in the easy style and manner, which do not draw too much from real life, require no deep effort or withdrawal to be understood, and send the reader back into the world full of noble sentiments and wise precepts applicable to every situation in human life. By means of such writings, virtue becomes attractive, science enjoyable, company instructive, and solitude entertaining.

Man is a reasoning being, and as such he draws his proper food and nourishment from science; but the limits of human understanding are so narrow that little satisfaction can be hoped for on this score, either from the breadth or the security of his acquisitions. Man is no less a sociable being than a reasoning one; but he cannot always enjoy agreeable and amusing company, or keep up the taste for it. Man is also an active being, and from this disposition, as well as from the various necessities of life, he must take up business and work; yet the mind needs some relaxation and cannot always sustain its bent for care and industry. It seems, then, that nature has marked out a mixed kind of life as best suited to the human race, and has quietly warned us not to let any of these inclinations _pull_ too strongly, lest they unfit us for our other occupations and pleasures. Indulge your passion for science, she says, but let your science be human, and have a direct bearing on action and society. Abstruse thought and profound research I forbid, and I shall severely punish, by the brooding melancholy they bring on, by the endless uncertainty they leave you in, and by the cold reception your supposed discoveries will meet when announced. Be a philosopher; but in all your philosophy, still be a man.

5. If most people were content to prefer the easy philosophy to the abstract and profound, without casting any blame or contempt on the latter, it might not be improper, perhaps, to go along with this general opinion and let every man enjoy his own taste and judgment without opposition. But since the matter is often pushed further, even to the outright rejection of all profound reasoning, or what is commonly called _metaphysics_, we shall now consider what can reasonably be said in its defense.

We may begin by noting that one significant advantage of the precise and abstract philosophy is the help it gives to the easy and humane one, which, without it, could never reach a sufficient level of exactness in its sentiments, precepts, or reasonings. All polite literature is nothing but a picture of human life in various attitudes and situations, inspiring us with different sentiments — praise or blame, admiration or ridicule — according to the qualities of the object it sets before us. An artist will be better qualified to succeed in this work if, beyond a delicate taste and quick perception, he also possesses an accurate knowledge of the inner workings of the understanding, the operations of the passions, and the various species of sentiment that distinguish vice from virtue. However painful this inward inquiry may seem, it is in some measure necessary for anyone who would describe with success the outward appearances of life and manners. The anatomist sets before the eye the most hideous and disagreeable objects, yet his science is useful to the painter even in delineating a Venus or a Helen. While the painter applies the richest colors of his art and gives his figures their most graceful and engaging airs, he must still attend to the inward structure of the human body, the placement of the muscles, the framework of the bones, and the use and shape of every part or organ. Accuracy is, in every case, an aid to beauty, and sound reasoning to refined sentiment. It is useless to elevate one by belittling the other.

We may also observe that in every art or profession, even those most concerned with practical life and action, a spirit of accuracy, however acquired, brings them all closer to perfection and makes them more useful to society. And though a philosopher may live remote from business, the spirit of philosophy, once carefully cultivated by enough people, must gradually spread through the whole of society and lend a similar precision to every art and calling. The politician will gain greater foresight and subtlety in dividing and balancing power; the lawyer more method and finer principles in his reasoning; and the general more regularity in his discipline and more caution in his plans and operations. The stability of modern governments over the ancient, and the accuracy of modern philosophy, have improved together, and will probably continue to improve, by similar gradual steps.

6. Even if no advantage could be gained from these studies beyond the satisfaction of an innocent curiosity, that alone would not be something to despise: it is one more addition to the few safe and harmless pleasures granted to the human race. The sweetest and most innocent path of life runs through the avenues of science and learning; and whoever can remove some obstacle along it, or open up some new prospect, deserves to be regarded as a benefactor to mankind. And though such research may appear painful and tiring, some minds are like some bodies — endowed with vigorous, blooming health, they require vigorous exercise and take pleasure in what most people would find burdensome and laborious. Obscurity is indeed painful to the mind as well as to the eye; but to bring light out of obscurity, by whatever labor, must be delightful and gratifying.

But this obscurity in the profound and abstract philosophy is objected to not only as painful and tiring but as the inevitable source of uncertainty and error. Here lies the fairest and most plausible objection against a large part of metaphysics: that it is not really a science but arises either from the fruitless efforts of human vanity, trying to penetrate subjects entirely beyond the understanding, or from the craft of popular superstitions, which, unable to defend themselves on open ground, raise these tangled thickets to shelter and protect their weakness. Driven out of the open country, these robbers flee into the forest and lie in wait to break in upon every unguarded avenue of the mind and overwhelm it with religious fears and prejudices. The stoutest opponent, if he relaxes his guard for a moment, is overcome. And many, through cowardice and folly, open the gates to the enemies and willingly receive them with reverence and submission, as their rightful sovereigns.

7. But is this a sufficient reason why philosophers should give up such research and leave superstition still in possession of her refuge? Should we not draw the opposite conclusion, and see the necessity of carrying the war into the most secret recesses of the enemy? It is vain to hope that men, from repeated disappointment, will at last give up such airy sciences and discover the proper province of human reason. For, beyond the fact that many people find too strong an interest in continually reviving such topics, the motive of blind despair can never reasonably have a place in the sciences: however unsuccessful past attempts may have been, there is still room to hope that the industry, good fortune, or sharper insight of later generations may reach discoveries unknown in earlier ages. Each adventurous mind will still leap at the arduous prize, finding himself stimulated rather than discouraged by the failures of his predecessors, hoping the glory of carrying through so hard an undertaking is reserved for him alone. The only way to free learning, once and for all, from these abstruse questions is to inquire seriously into the nature of human understanding and to show, through an exact analysis of its powers and capacity, that it is by no means equipped for such remote and abstruse subjects. We must submit to this effort in order to live at ease afterward, and must cultivate true metaphysics carefully in order to destroy the false and adulterated kind. Indolence, which for some people serves as a safeguard against this deceptive philosophy, is in others outweighed by curiosity; and despair, which sometimes prevails, may later give way to confident hopes and expectations. Accurate and sound reasoning is the only universal remedy, fitted for all persons and all dispositions; it alone can overturn that abstruse philosophy and metaphysical jargon which, mixed up with popular superstition, becomes nearly impenetrable to careless reasoners and takes on the appearance of science and wisdom.

8. Besides this advantage of rejecting, after careful inquiry, the most uncertain and unpleasant part of learning, there are many positive benefits to be had from a precise examination of the powers and faculties of human nature. It is striking that the operations of the mind, though most intimately present to us, seem wrapped in obscurity whenever they become the object of reflection; nor can the eye readily find the lines and boundaries that distinguish them from one another. The objects are too fine to stay long in the same aspect or position, and must be grasped in an instant, by a superior insight given by nature and improved by habit and reflection. It becomes, then, no small part of science simply to know the different operations of the mind, to separate them from each other, to classify them under their proper heads, and to correct the apparent disorder in which they lie when made the object of reflection and inquiry. This work of ordering and distinguishing, which has no special merit when applied to external bodies, the objects of our senses, gains in value when directed at the operations of the mind, in proportion to the difficulty and labor it requires. And even if we can go no further than this mental geography, or sketching of the distinct parts and powers of the mind, it is at least a satisfaction to go that far; and the more obvious this science may appear (and it is by no means obvious), the more contemptible must ignorance of it be reckoned in all who lay claim to learning and philosophy.

Nor can there remain any suspicion that this science is uncertain and fanciful, unless we entertain a skepticism so radical as to undermine all speculation, and even all action. It cannot be doubted that the mind is endowed with several powers and faculties, that these powers are distinct from one another, that what is genuinely distinct to immediate perception can be distinguished by reflection, and therefore that there is a truth and falsehood in all propositions on this subject — a truth and falsehood that lie within the reach of human understanding. There are many obvious distinctions of this kind, such as those between will and understanding, imagination and the passions, which fall within the comprehension of every human creature; and the finer, more philosophical distinctions are no less real and certain, though more difficult to grasp. Some recent instances of success in these inquiries may give us a juster sense of the certainty and solidity of this branch of learning. And shall we count it worthy of a philosopher's labor to give us an accurate system of the planets and settle the position and order of those remote bodies, while we pretend to overlook those who, with so much success, map out the parts of the mind, in which we are so deeply concerned?

9. But may we not hope that philosophy, if cultivated with care and encouraged by public attention, may push its inquiries still further, and discover, at least to some degree, the hidden springs and principles by which the human mind is moved in its operations? Astronomers had long been content to establish, from the phenomena, the true motions, order, and size of the heavenly bodies; until at last a philosopher arose who seems, through the most fortunate reasoning, to have also determined the laws and forces by which the revolutions of the planets are governed and directed. The same has been done in other parts of nature. And there is no reason to despair of equal success in our inquiries into the powers and economy of the mind, if pursued with equal ability and care. It is likely that one operation and principle of the mind depends on another, which in turn may be reduced to one still more general and universal; and how far these inquiries can be carried it will be hard to determine exactly, before, or even after, a careful trial. This much is certain: attempts of this kind are made every day, even by those who philosophize most carelessly; and nothing can be more necessary than to undertake the project with thorough care and attention, so that, if it lies within the compass of human understanding, it may at last be successfully achieved, and if not, may at least be set aside with some confidence and security. This last conclusion is surely not desirable, nor should it be embraced too hastily. For how much would we lose of the beauty and value of this kind of philosophy on such an assumption? Moralists, when they considered the vast variety of actions that excite our approval or disapproval, have so far been used to searching for some common principle on which this diversity of sentiments might depend. And though they have sometimes pushed the matter too far, in their eagerness for a single general principle, it must be admitted that they are excusable in expecting to find some general principles into which all vices and virtues might justly be resolved. Critics, logicians, and even politicians have made similar efforts, and their attempts have not been wholly unsuccessful, though more time, greater accuracy, and more ardent application may bring these sciences still closer to perfection. To abandon all such ambitions at once would justly be considered more rash, hasty, and dogmatic than even the boldest and most assertive philosophy that ever tried to impose its crude pronouncements and principles on mankind.

10. What if these reasonings about human nature seem abstract and hard to grasp? That gives no presumption of their falsehood. On the contrary, it seems impossible that what has so far escaped so many wise and profound philosophers can be very obvious or easy. And whatever pains such research may cost us, we may consider ourselves sufficiently rewarded, in pleasure as well as profit, if by this means we can add anything to our stock of knowledge on subjects of such unspeakable importance.

But since, after all, the abstractness of these speculations is no recommendation but rather a disadvantage to them, and since this difficulty may perhaps be overcome by care and skill and the avoidance of unnecessary detail, we have, in the following enquiry, tried to shed some light on subjects from which uncertainty has so far deterred the wise, and obscurity the ignorant. Happy, if we can unite the boundaries of the different species of philosophy, by reconciling profound inquiry with clarity, and truth with novelty! And happier still, if, reasoning in this accessible way, we can undermine the foundations of an abstruse philosophy which seems so far to have served only as a shelter for superstition and a cover for absurdity and error!

chapters.title: Section 2: OF THE ORIGIN OF IDEAS.
paragraphs: 11. Everyone will readily admit that there is a considerable difference between the perceptions of the mind when a man feels the pain of excessive heat or the pleasure of moderate warmth, and when he afterwards recalls that sensation from memory or anticipates it in his imagination. These faculties may mimic or copy the perceptions of the senses, but they can never fully match the force and vividness of the original feeling. The most we can say of them, even when they operate with the greatest vigor, is that they represent their object so lively that we could _almost_ say we feel or see it. But unless the mind is disordered by disease or madness, they can never reach such a pitch of vivacity as to make these perceptions wholly indistinguishable. All the colors of poetry, however splendid, can never paint natural objects in such a way as to make the description be taken for a real landscape. The liveliest thought is still inferior to the dullest sensation.

We may observe a similar distinction running through all the other perceptions of the mind. A man in a fit of anger is moved very differently from one who merely thinks about that emotion. If you tell me that someone is in love, I easily grasp your meaning and form a correct conception of his situation, but I can never mistake that conception for the real turmoil and agitation of the passion. When we reflect on our past feelings and affections, our thought is a faithful mirror that copies its objects truthfully; but the colors it uses are faint and dull compared with those in which our original perceptions were clothed. No fine discernment or metaphysical mind is needed to mark the distinction between them.

12. Here, then, we may divide all the perceptions of the mind into two classes or species, distinguished by their different degrees of force and vividness. The less forcible and lively are commonly called _Thoughts_ or _Ideas_. The other species lacks a name in our language, and in most others — I suppose because there was no need, except for philosophical purposes, to group them under a general term. Let us therefore take a small liberty and call them _Impressions_, using the word in a sense somewhat different from the usual one. By the term _impression_, then, I mean all our more lively perceptions, when we hear, or see, or feel, or love, or hate, or desire, or will. And impressions are distinguished from ideas, which are the less lively perceptions of which we are conscious when we reflect on any of those sensations or movements just mentioned.

13. Nothing, at first glance, may seem more unbounded than the thought of man, which not only escapes all human power and authority but is not even restrained within the limits of nature and reality. To form monsters, and join incongruous shapes and appearances, costs the imagination no more trouble than to conceive the most natural and familiar objects. And while the body is confined to one planet, along which it creeps with pain and difficulty, thought can in an instant transport us to the most distant regions of the universe, or even beyond the universe, into the unbounded chaos where nature is supposed to lie in total confusion. What was never seen, or heard of, may yet be conceived; nor is anything beyond the power of thought, except what implies an absolute contradiction.

But although our thought seems to possess this unbounded liberty, we shall find on closer examination that it is in fact confined within very narrow limits, and that all this creative power of the mind amounts to no more than the capacity for combining, transposing, augmenting, or diminishing the materials supplied to us by the senses and experience. When we think of a golden mountain, we only join two consistent ideas, _gold_ and _mountain_, with which we were already acquainted. We can conceive of a virtuous horse because, from our own feeling, we can conceive virtue, and we may unite this with the figure and shape of a horse, an animal familiar to us. In short, all the materials of thinking are derived either from our outward or inward sentiment: the mixing and composing of these belongs to the mind and will alone. Or, to put it in philosophical language, all our ideas, or fainter perceptions, are copies of our impressions, or livelier ones.

14. To prove this, the following two arguments will, I hope, be sufficient. First, when we analyze our thoughts or ideas, however compounded or sublime, we always find that they resolve into such simple ideas as were copied from a prior feeling or sentiment. Even those ideas which at first sight seem most remote from this origin are found, on closer scrutiny, to derive from it. The idea of God, taken as an infinitely intelligent, wise, and good Being, arises from reflecting on the operations of our own mind and increasing, without limit, those qualities of goodness and wisdom. We may push this enquiry as far as we like; we shall always find that every idea we examine is copied from a similar impression. Those who would assert that this position is not universally true, and admits exceptions, have only one — and that an easy — way of refuting it: by producing the idea which, in their opinion, is not derived from this source. It will then be incumbent on us, if we wish to maintain our doctrine, to produce the impression, or lively perception, that corresponds to it.

15. Secondly. If it should happen, through a defect of the organ, that a man is incapable of any species of sensation, we always find that he is equally incapable of the corresponding ideas. A blind man can form no notion of colors; a deaf man, none of sounds. Restore to either of them the sense in which he is deficient: by opening this new inlet for his sensations, you also open an inlet for the ideas, and he has no difficulty conceiving these objects. The same is true if the object proper for exciting some sensation has simply never been applied to the organ. A Laplander or a Negro has no notion of the taste of wine. And though there are few or no instances of a similar deficiency in the mind — where a person has never felt, or is wholly incapable of, a sentiment or passion belonging to his species — we find the same observation holding in lesser degree. A man of mild manners can form no idea of inveterate revenge or cruelty; nor can a selfish heart easily conceive the heights of friendship and generosity. It is readily granted that other beings may possess many senses of which we can have no conception, because the ideas of them have never been introduced to us in the only way an idea can reach the mind — namely, by actual feeling and sensation.

16. There is, however, one contradictory phenomenon that may prove it is not absolutely impossible for ideas to arise independently of their corresponding impressions. It will readily be granted, I believe, that the several distinct ideas of color which enter by the eye, or of sound which are conveyed by the ear, are really different from one another, though resembling. Now if this is true of different colors, it must be no less true of the different shades of the same color: each shade produces a distinct idea, independent of the rest. For if this were denied, it would be possible, by the continual gradation of shades, to run a color insensibly into its most distant counterpart; and if you will not allow any of the intermediate steps to be different, you cannot, without absurdity, deny that the extremes are the same. Suppose, then, that a person has enjoyed his sight for thirty years and has become perfectly acquainted with colors of all kinds except one particular shade of blue, for instance, which he has never happened to encounter. Place before him all the different shades of that color except that single one, descending gradually from the deepest to the lightest. It is plain he will perceive a blank where that shade is missing, and will be aware that the distance at that point between the adjacent colors is greater than anywhere else. Now I ask: is it possible for him, from his own imagination, to supply this deficiency and raise up the idea of that particular shade, though it had never been conveyed to him by his senses? I believe there are few who will not think he can; and this may serve as proof that the simple ideas are not always, in every instance, derived from the corresponding impressions. But this instance is so singular that it scarcely warrants our attention, and does not merit that we should alter our general maxim for its sake alone.

17. Here, then, is a proposition that not only seems, in itself, simple and intelligible, but which, if put to proper use, might render every dispute equally intelligible, and banish all the jargon that has for so long taken possession of metaphysical reasonings and brought disgrace upon them. All ideas, especially abstract ones, are naturally faint and obscure: the mind has only a slender hold on them; they are easily confused with other resembling ideas; and when we have often used a term, even without a distinct meaning, we are apt to imagine it has a determinate idea attached to it. By contrast, all impressions — that is, all sensations, whether outward or inward — are strong and vivid: the limits between them are more exactly fixed, and it is not easy to fall into error or mistake about them. Whenever, then, we suspect that a philosophical term is being used without any meaning or idea (as is all too common), we need only ask: _from what impression is that supposed idea derived_? And if no impression can be supplied, this will serve to confirm our suspicion. By bringing ideas into so clear a light, we may reasonably hope to dispel every dispute that may arise concerning their nature and reality.[1]

[1] What those who denied innate ideas probably meant was no more than that all ideas are copies of our impressions; though it must be admitted that the terms they used were not chosen with sufficient caution, nor so exactly defined, as to prevent every mistake about their doctrine. For what is meant by _innate_? If innate is equivalent to natural, then all the perceptions and ideas of the mind must be granted to be innate or natural, in whatever sense we take the latter word — whether in opposition to what is uncommon, artificial, or miraculous. If by innate is meant contemporary with our birth, the dispute seems frivolous; nor is it worthwhile to enquire at what point thinking begins — before, at, or after our birth. Again, the word _idea_ seems commonly to be taken in a very loose sense by LOCKE and others, as standing for any of our perceptions — our sensations and passions as well as thoughts. Now in this sense, I should like to know what can be meant by asserting that self-love, or resentment of injuries, or the passion between the sexes is not innate.

But admitting these terms, _impressions_ and _ideas_, in the sense explained above, and understanding by _innate_ what is original, or copied from no prior perception, then we may assert that all our impressions are innate, and our ideas are not innate.

To be candid, I must own it as my opinion that LOCKE was led into this question by the schoolmen, who, by making use of undefined terms, draw out their disputes to a tedious length without ever touching the point at issue. A similar ambiguity and circumlocution seem to run through that philosopher's reasonings on this as on most other subjects.

chapters.title: Section 3: OF THE ASSOCIATION OF IDEAS.
paragraphs: 18. It is evident that there is a principle of connection between the different thoughts or ideas of the mind, and that, as they appear in memory or imagination, they introduce one another with a certain degree of method and regularity. In our more serious thinking or discourse this is so observable that any particular thought breaking in upon the regular track or chain of ideas is immediately noticed and rejected. And even in our wildest and most wandering reveries, indeed in our very dreams, we shall find, if we reflect, that the imagination was not running purely at random, but that some connection was still maintained among the different ideas that succeeded one another. Were the loosest and freest conversation to be transcribed, something would at once be observed connecting it through all its transitions. Or, where this seems absent, the person who broke the thread of discourse could still tell you that a succession of thoughts had secretly turned in his mind, gradually leading him away from the subject of conversation. Across different languages, even where we cannot suspect the least connection or contact, it is found that the words expressive of even the most compounded ideas correspond very nearly to one another: a sure proof that the simple ideas contained in the compound ones were bound together by some universal principle which had an equal influence on all mankind.

19. Though it is too obvious to escape notice that different ideas are connected together, I do not find that any philosopher has tried to enumerate or classify all the principles of association — a subject, however, that seems worth curiosity. To me, there appear to be only three principles of connection among ideas, namely: _Resemblance_, _Contiguity_ in time or place, and _Cause or Effect_.

That these principles serve to connect ideas will, I believe, scarcely be doubted. A picture naturally leads our thoughts to the original[2]; the mention of one room in a building naturally prompts inquiry or discourse about the others[3]; and if we think of a wound, we can hardly help reflecting on the pain that follows it[4]. But that this list is complete, and that there are no other principles of association besides these, may be hard to prove to the reader's satisfaction, or even to one's own. All we can do in such cases is run through several instances and examine carefully the principle that binds the different thoughts together, never stopping until we make the principle as general as possible[5]. The more instances we examine, and the more care we employ, the more assurance we acquire that the list we draw up from the whole is complete.

[5] For instance, Contrast or Contrariety is also a connection among Ideas; but it may perhaps be regarded as a mixture of _Causation_ and _Resemblance_. Where two objects are contrary, the one destroys the other; that is, it is the cause of its annihilation, and the idea of the annihilation of an object implies the idea of its former existence.
